title: The Green Revolution worldwide
summary: Two decades of wheat research in Mexico produced high-yielding dwarf varieties and new production methods. By 1970 Norman Borlaug, who received that year's Nobel Peace Prize, reported tremendous progress in cereal production in India, Pakistan and the Philippines over the past three years. FAO calls him the father of the Green Revolution, which improved food security worldwide and saved millions from starvation.

uncertainty.note: Breeding breakthroughs developed in Mexico spread internationally in the 1960s; Norman Borlaug was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in December 1970.

where.modern_name: Worldwide; stand-in pin in Mexico, where the wheat varieties were bred
where.historical_name: Texcoco, State of Mexico, United Mexican States

importance.justification: New crop varieties and methods sharply raised grain production in several developing countries.

related.because: Surging twentieth-century world population created acute food supply deficits that spurred international investments in high-yielding dwarf grain varieties.

sources.title: Norman Borlaug: Nobel Lecture, The Green Revolution, Peace, and Humanity
sources.author: Norman E. Borlaug

reviewer_note: These sources praise Borlaug and do not cover the environmental and social costs that critics raise. Dates mark what his lecture reports. The pin in Mexico is a stand-in.
